opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd put it simply: we want to build AI that actually understands the world, not just AI that's very good at producing language.

Large language models have been remarkably successful, and I don't want to downplay that. But I think we've gotten used to equating intelligence with text. Most of what intelligence is, in humans and animals, has nothing to do with language. A cat can't write an essay, but it understands physics, objects, cause and effect, and how to plan in a messy, continuous world far better than any current model. That kind of grounded understanding is what's missing, and that's what we care about.

So the central mission is building world models: systems that learn from rich sensory data, especially video and interaction, form an internal representation of how the world works, and use it to predict, reason, and plan. Yann has argued for this for years, the idea that you shouldn't predict every pixel but should predict in an abstract representation space, the way we do. My own background is in visual representation learning, so for me this is a continuation of a question I've cared about for a long time: what is the right way for a machine to see and to learn from seeing?

There's also a practical side. If you want AI that works in the physical world, in robotics, in science, in anything where the real world pushes back, autoregressive next-token prediction alone probably won't get you there. You need models with persistent memory, the ability to reason about consequences, and real controllability and safety, because you can specify objectives and the system plans toward them instead of improvising word by word.

Part of the mission is also how we do it. We want to stay close to open research, publish, and work with the community, because a problem this hard won't be solved by one lab behind closed doors. For me personally, it's a bet. It's a long-horizon, somewhat contrarian bet, but I think it's the right question for this moment, and that's what makes it exciting.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes building world models as the mission, but does not identify a research breakthrough as the company’s ultimate product.

r002.rationale: It says the goal is AI that understands the world and contrasts this with AI focused on producing language, including language models.

r003.rationale: The candidate calls the work a long-horizon bet but does not compare its intended significance to Transformers or ChatGPT.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it, the mission comes down to one word that Yann has been repeating for years: world models. Everything we're building is organized around that idea.

Let me explain what I mean. The dominant paradigm right now is language models, and they're remarkable. But if you step back and ask what intelligence actually is, language is a fairly thin layer on top of something much deeper. A baby understands that objects persist when they go out of view, that things fall when you drop them, that a cup will spill if you tilt it, long before it can say a single word. Animals have rich models of the physical world without any language at all. That understanding, how the world works, what will happen next, what the consequences of an action are, is what we call a world model. And current systems, for all their fluency, largely don't have it.

So the central mission, as I understand it, is to build machines that learn how the world works primarily by observing it, the way humans and animals do, rather than by reading text about it. That means learning from video, from sensory data, from interaction. It means learning representations where the model can predict in an abstract space instead of trying to reproduce every pixel. This is the JEPA line of thinking that Yann has pushed, and a lot of my own research on visual representation learning points in the same direction.

There's a second part of the mission that I care about just as much, which is openness. Yann and I both come from a tradition where research is shared, where you publish, you release code, you let the community poke holes in your work. I think the field has drifted away from that, and I think that drift is actually bad for progress. Part of why we started this company was to create a place where ambitious, long-horizon research can happen and where the results can go back out into the world.

And I'll be honest, this is a bet. It's not the path of least resistance. The easier thing would be to take a language model, scale it, and ship products. We're saying that the next real leap in intelligence requires a different foundation, that perception and physical understanding have to come first, and that reasoning and planning should sit on top of a grounded model of reality rather than on top of text statistics. If we're right, the payoff is systems that can actually operate in the real world, in robotics, in science, in situations where there's no training corpus to memorize. That's what gets me out of bed.

r001.rationale: The response describes world models and real-world systems as the mission and payoff, but does not identify a research breakthrough as the company’s ultimate product.

r002.rationale: It says the next leap requires a different foundation from scaling language models, centered on learning how the world works through observation and interaction.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison to Transformers or ChatGPT, or claim that the intended breakthrough would be comparable in significance.

astra-6.text: For me, the central mission is to pursue the fundamental research that makes more capable AI possible, and to turn that research into something useful. Those two parts have to stay connected: a long-term scientific ambition, and a clear sense of what progress enables people to do. That’s the way I think about what we’re building together.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about our mission is to build AI that can understand the physical world, predict what might happen, and use that understanding to plan and act. Language is an important part of intelligence, but a lot of what humans know comes from observing and interacting with the world, rather than reading descriptions of it.

So the central research question is: how can a machine learn a useful model of the world from those observations? And “useful” doesn’t necessarily mean predicting every pixel. It means capturing the things that matter for reasoning and making decisions.

For me, that connects the scientific goal with the practical one. We want to understand how to build that kind of intelligence, and ultimately make it useful in systems that can help people in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes building useful AI systems, but does not identify a research breakthrough as the company’s ultimate product.

r002.rationale: It contrasts learning from physical-world observations with relying on language descriptions, but does not state that the company seeks a breakthrough fundamentally different from language models.

r003.rationale: The response makes no comparison to Transformers or ChatGPT, or to breakthroughs of comparable significance.
